hook: The grandson of Genghis Khan who conquered China and built the city that became Beijing.

pages.x: Kublai was born in 1215, a grandson of Genghis Khan. His mother Sorghaghtani, a Christian and a brilliant manager, made sure he learned about China and the people his family ruled, and found him Chinese advisers.

When his brother, the Great Khan Mongke, died in 1259, Kublai and his youngest brother each claimed the throne. Kublai won the civil war in 1264, but the Mongol Empire split into four separate realms.

In 1271 he founded a Chinese-style dynasty, the Yuan, and built a new capital, Dadu, on the site of Beijing. In 1279 he finished conquering the Song dynasty in the south. For the first time, all of China was ruled by a foreigner.

His summer capital, Shangdu, had a marble palace and a park full of deer and streams. Marco Polo described it, and 500 years later the poet Coleridge woke from a dream and wrote: "In Xanadu did Kubla Khan a stately pleasure-dome decree".
Twice he sent huge fleets to invade Japan, in 1274 and 1281. Both times typhoons smashed the ships. The Japanese called the storms kamikaze, "divine wind".

pages.t: A court open to the world
pages.x: Kublai welcomed Muslims, Christians, Buddhists and Taoists, and gave foreigners high posts, partly because he did not fully trust his Chinese officials. A young Venetian, Marco Polo, served him for 17 years and described his court to amazed Europeans.
Kublai Khan reunited China after 300 years of division and founded the Yuan dynasty. His capital became today's Beijing, and through Marco Polo his court made China known in Europe.
pts: Built the city that became Beijing
